newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Explosion outside OSCE, UN office in Serb town.
newsitem.headline: Explosion outside OSCE, UN office in Serb town.

text.p: A bomb blast destroyed an OSCE truck but caused no casualties outside offices of international monitors in Serb-controlled Bosnia, a U.N. official said on Monday.

"There was a sizeable explosion about 30 metres (yards) from the building which houses both the U.N. and the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe in Zvornik," United Nations spokesman Liam McDowall said.
"The blast completely destroyed one OSCE vehicle and damaged a second civilian vehicle nearby," he told Reuters.

The explosion occurred on Sunday evening in the eastern town of Zvornik in Bosnia's Serb entity just days after NATO soldiers swooped on two Serbs indicted by the U.N. war crimes tribunal in The Hague.
British special forces in the northwest Prijedor region arrested one suspect last Thursday and shot dead another who opened fire on soldiers trying to detain him.

Serb authorities held an official funeral on Sunday for Simo Drljaca, a notorious police chief in Prijedor accused of conducting brutal "ethnic cleansing" against Moslems and Croats during the Bosnian war.
The 9.40 p.m. (1940 GMT) blast in Zvornik shattered windows in buildings and carved a 20-cm (eight-inch) hole in the ground, an OSCE official said.
Initial reports indicated that two to six kg (four to 13 pounds) of plastic explosives were placed under the engine of the OSCE truck, the official said.
It was parked in front of the Hotel Drina, which serves as local headquarters for the U.N. and the OSCE. The hotel sits on a bluff overlooking the Drina River, which forms the border with Serbia.
Zvornik is ruled by hardline Serb nationalists loyal to Radovan Karadzic, the former Bosnian Serb president and an indicted war criminal.
McDowall said U.N. police monitors were investigating whether the bomb was a response to NATO pouncing on Serb war-crimes suspects raid or was the result of a dispute among local mafia.
Until Sunday night, the NATO-led peace force and the U.N. mission in Bosnia had reported no violent backlash in Serb territory since the British swoop last Thursday.
U.N. police monitors did report cases of minor harassment in Serb territory over the weekend, with bottles thrown at U.N. staff and threats to landlords housing international police officers.
McDowall said the United Nations had adopted "additional security precautions in the immediate Zvornik region" but declined to specify what measures were taken.
